THOUGHT: The patient is a 59-year-old male with sudden-onset, brief (3-minute), positional vertigo—specifically triggered by lying back with head turned to the left—accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and reproducible nystagmus. Crucially, the Dix-Hallpike maneuver is positive on the left side, eliciting both vertigo and characteristic nystagmus (torsional-upbeating, geotropic, fatigable, latency <20 sec), which is the gold-standard diagnostic test for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). The absence of red-flag symptoms—no headache, hearing loss, tinnitus, neurological deficits, or gait instability—and normal head imaging (ruling out stroke, tumor, or structural lesion), normal audiometry, and lack of persistent symptoms between episodes further support a peripheral, canalolithiasis-based etiology rather than central causes (e.g., posterior circulation stroke, vestibular neuritis, or MS). While vestibular neuritis can cause acute vertigo, it is typically prolonged (days), non-positional, and associated with unidirectional horizontal nystagmus without latency or fatigability—and would not be Dix-Hallpike–positive. Similarly, Meniere’s disease usually presents with recurrent episodes plus auditory symptoms (hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness), which are absent here. The age (peak incidence 50–70 years), first-time presentation, and classic positional trigger strongly favor BPPV—most commonly involving the posterior semicircular canal (accounting for >80% of BPPV cases).

DIAGNOSIS: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
